1.pericope_label: Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart: but as for me, my feet were almost gone

schools.summary: Augustine works on a form of the inscription which says that the hymns of David the son of Jesse have failed, notes that nowhere else is the father’s name added, and holds that a hymn must have three things, praise, praise of God, and singing, so that a failure of hymns is a painful thing to report.

Gill allows the Israel of the first verse to be both the nation and the people God has chosen and called, and hears in the second the confession of an ungrateful creature who had received a thousand kindnesses; Calvin sets out the argument of the whole psalm in four movements, the praise of God’s righteousness, the shock of seeing the wicked abound while the godly pine away, the reproof of his own rashness in judging from the present state of things, and the conclusion that providence must be left to take its course by the degrees determined in the secret purpose of God.

Henry reads the abrupt opening as a man checking himself while the fire burned in his musing, and sets the principle he holds to beside three others, the omniscience of God on which one sufferer fixed, the justice of God on which a prophet fixed, the holiness of God on which another fixed, and the goodness of God here; Spurgeon renders the first word only rather than truly, opens the second verse as a spiritual battle in which the half-defeated became wholly victorious, and marks the connection between the heart and the feet, since when men doubt the righteousness of God their own integrity begins to waver.

Clarke ascribes the psalm to the singer named in the title, places him under the captivity and takes the psalm as consolation for a people in bondage who saw a more corrupt nation prospering over them, and states plainly that the writer had nearly given up his confidence and was ready to find fault with providence; Wesley keeps the first verse to the true Israelites who serve God in spirit and truth and makes the slipping feet his faith in providence almost overthrown.

Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm in its collection as the first of a group of eleven and the counterpart of an earlier one, hold against a scholar that the temptation is not toward heathenism but toward free-thinking, and note that its doubts about the moral order are set at rest as in two other psalms and in the book of Job; Ellicott makes the opening particle a rejoinder to something supposed, quotes an English poet on virtue in distress and vice in triumph making atheists of mankind, argues that the second clause limits the first since a moral correspondence with their profession is necessary even in the chosen people, and glosses the slipping as literally being poured out.

debates: Does the first verse say truly or only? Spurgeon renders it only, so that God is nothing else but good to his own, his goodness beyond dispute and without mixture. Ellicott takes the particle as a rejoinder to a supposed statement, like the Latin word it answers to, and reads the verse as an answer to an objection rather than a plain assertion. On the second clause he holds that it limits the first rather than repeating it, since the subject of the psalm requires that a moral correspondence be necessary even in the chosen people; Gill and Wesley allow the wider and the narrower Israel together.
outliers: Ellicott answers the psalm’s complaint with an English poet’s lines, that virtue in distress and vice in triumph make atheists of mankind.
Henry sets the psalmist’s anchoring principle beside three others, the omniscience, the justice and the holiness of God on which three earlier sufferers fixed, this one fixing on his goodness.
Augustine takes the failing of the hymns as his subject and defines what a hymn requires, praise, praise of God, and singing, so that the loss of one is a thing to be deplored.
Spurgeon draws a practical connection between doctrine and conduct, that when men doubt the righteousness of God their own integrity begins to waver.
themes: a father’s name added only here
a fire that burned while he mused

3.pericope_label: For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked: for there are no bands in their death: therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain

schools.summary: Gill identifies the foolish from a Jewish writer as the atheists who deny the creation, men wise in things natural and without understanding in things spiritual, offers two renderings of the fourth verse and notes a Latin version in which they pay their death no regard, and takes the chain of pride for bondage, since those under its power are its slaves though they bind it about themselves fancying it an ornament, tracing the sin from the devils and the first parents to Sodom.

Clarke answers the envy with a heathen maxim that the prosperity of the wicked is a reproach to the gods, and with the argument that man could not bear prosperity, since if men had uninterrupted comforts here perhaps not one soul would seek a preparation for heaven; he contrasts the sore conflicts of the godly at death with the ungodly whom Satan does not molest, being sure of his prey, sees in the chain of pride an allusion to the golden ensigns of magistracy, and doubts the English of the seventh verse, preferring that they surpass the thoughts of their own heart; Wesley makes the bands of the fourth verse judicial, since such men are not dragged to death by the sentence of the magistrate.

Ellicott corrects the foolish to the arrogant and suggests that the verb rendered saw is synonymous with envied, calls the fourth verse quite unintelligible as it stands and holds that some emendation is absolutely necessary, reporting a conjecture that by one letter yields no bands to their yoke and makes the men chartered libertines, and renders the sixth verse that pride is their necklace and violence their mantle; Keil and Delitzsch prefer a variant favoured by three scholars and the Greek, in which iniquity presses forth out of a fat heart, granting that the parallelism decides for it.

debates: What does the fourth verse say? Ellicott calls the English quite unintelligible and no fair rendering of the Hebrew, rejects the sense of a painless death as out of keeping with the psalm, finds no help in the ancient versions, and holds that emendation is absolutely necessary, reporting a conjecture that changes one letter to give no bands to their yoke. Keil and Delitzsch prefer a different variant, in which the iniquity of such men presses forth out of a fat heart, and hold that the parallelism decides for it. Wesley, Gill and Clarke keep the received text and divide over whether the bands are judicial, physical or spiritual.
outliers: Clarke argues that prosperity would be bad for us, since if men had uninterrupted comforts here perhaps not one soul would ever seek a preparation for heaven, so that the warfare of human life is the highest proof of a benevolent providence.
Ellicott reports a conjectural emendation of one letter that turns the wicked from men who die painlessly into men who wear no yoke at all, chartered libertines.
Clarke observes that corpulency obliterates the natural lines of the face, so that little remains beside the human hog.
Clarke doubts the familiar rendering that they have more than heart could wish, asking whose heart ever said it had enough that had not its portion in God.
themes: a verse that must be emended
death without a sigh or a groan
more than they expected, not more than they wish

9.pericope_label: They set their mouth against the heavens: therefore his people return hither: they say, how doth God know? behold, these are the ungodly, who prosper in the world

schools.summary: Gill takes the heavens of the ninth verse for God and lists what such men speak against, his being, perfections, decrees and providence, reporting a Jewish interpreter who understands the angels and a version that understands the saints; he offers three constructions of the tenth verse, the true people of God returning to the same temptation, professors returning to the company of the wicked, or the followers of the wicked returning to their leaders; and he removes one misunderstanding of the eleventh, since the question is not about the manner of God’s knowing but about his knowledge itself.

Clarke enumerates the acts of the ninth verse, blaspheming God, ridiculing religion, mocking at providence and laughing at a future state, writes that very few verses in the Bible have been more variously translated than the tenth and sets out four renderings of it, and gives both possibilities for the eleventh, that the people stumbled by prosperity say God cannot know or that the wicked themselves say he knows nothing of their doings; Wesley keeps the walking tongue to a liberty that reproaches all sorts of persons and has the followers partaking of their leaders’ prosperity.

Ellicott renders the preposition of the ninth verse in rather than against, making the verse a picture of pride vaunting to the skies and trumpeting its praises through the world, and prefers for the tenth the reading of an old English prayer book, which rests on the Hebrew margin and describes the popularity such self-applause gains; Keil and Delitzsch say that for such men doubt becomes the transition to apostasy, that the poet resolved the riddle in a wholly different way, and refuse two proposed emendations of the fifteenth verse since prepositions are sometimes used elliptically.

debates: How is the tenth verse to be translated? Clarke says very few verses in the Bible have been more variously rendered, and that the translators have blown the hot to cool it and the cold to warm it; he sets out four renderings, from the people of God falling off to such men and profiting by it, to their being squeezed until the juice is wrung out of their bodies, to a version that has them bruised with mallets. Ellicott prefers the reading of an old English prayer book, resting on the Hebrew margin, in which the people turn to these men and a cup of adulation is sucked out by them. Gill offers three constructions of his own and Wesley takes the simplest.
outliers: Clarke measures the difficulty of the tenth verse by the number of its renderings, saying that the translators have blown the hot to cool it and the cold to warm it.
Ellicott turns the ninth verse from blasphemy into self-advertisement, a mouth set in the heavens while the tongue walks through the earth.
Keil and Delitzsch state where the argument of the psalm stands at this point, that for such men doubt becomes the transition to apostasy.

Gill distinguishes the question of the eleventh verse from a question about the manner of God’s knowing, since he knows neither by sense nor by reasoning but beholds all things in his own eternal mind.
themes: a mouth set in the heavens
doubt on the road to apostasy

15.pericope_label: If I say, I will speak thus; behold, I should offend against the generation of thy children: until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end

schools.summary: Henry counts the silence of the fifteenth verse the first point gained in the victory, since respect for the people of God restrained the writer from uttering what he had conceived; Spurgeon turns the same into a rule, that thoughts kept within injure only ourselves while once uttered their mischief may be great, and that from such a man the utterance would have been a heavy blow to the whole brotherhood, his second thoughts being by far the best.

Gill says the reconciling was attempted by the mere dint of reason without consulting the sacred oracles or experience, takes the sanctuary plainly for the house where the word was read and prayer made, notes that some understand by it the Scriptures themselves, and draws the lesson that the temptation did not so far prevail as to make the man neglect public worship, which is the very means of relief under doubts.

Clarke puts the fifteenth verse as a discovery that the writer had reasoned incorrectly against the uniform testimony of all the children of God, fills the failure of the sixteenth with the history of their fathers while admitting that the continuance of the captivity puzzles him again, raises against his own dating the objection that a psalm written in exile can hardly speak of going into a sanctuary that was destroyed, and states the conclusion as a discovery that the present is a state of trial and the prosperity of the wicked a prelude to their destruction; Wesley defines the offence as grieving and discouraging the people of God and takes the sanctuary of the practice of resorting to the oracle in difficult cases.

Ellicott renders the fifteenth verse with two finite verbs for one thought as the Hebrew often does, glosses the verb of the sixteenth as reflecting in order to know, and makes the sanctuary the service itself, where the blessings and warnings read from the law or chanted from an ancient song turned the writer’s thoughts to consequences, though still to consequences in this world, the thought of a hereafter not having established itself sufficiently to have an ethical force; Keil and Delitzsch mark the change of standpoint, the poet calming himself with the solution and placing himself at the standpoint of the end.

debates: What is the sanctuary of the seventeenth verse? Gill takes it for the house of God where the word was read and prayer made, and notes that some understand the Scriptures instead; Wesley for the practice of resorting to the oracle in difficult cases; Ellicott for the Temple service, whose readings and songs turned the writer’s thoughts to consequences. Clarke raises the historical objection against his own dating of the psalm, that if it was written during the captivity there was no sanctuary in the land of exile and the one at home had long been destroyed.
outliers: Clarke raises an objection to his own dating of the psalm, asking how a writer in exile can speak of entering a sanctuary that was destroyed.
Ellicott limits what the writer saw in the sanctuary to consequences in this world, holding that the thought of a hereafter had not yet established itself sufficiently to have an ethical force.
Spurgeon draws a rule of speech from the fifteenth verse, that thoughts kept within injure only ourselves while once uttered their mischief may be great.
Gill turns the seventeenth verse into an argument for public worship, since the temptation never so far prevailed as to keep the man from the house of God, which is the means of relief under doubt.
themes: a sanctuary in a land of exile
consequences, but only in this world

21.pericope_label: Thus my heart was grieved, and I was pricked in my reins: nevertheless I am continually with thee: whom have I in heaven but thee?

schools.summary: Henry calls the passage an old riddle unriddled again, meat out of the eater and sweetness out of the strong, since the writer made a good improvement of the temptation that had almost overcome him, and observes that a man who stumbles without falling takes the longer steps for recovering himself, God not suffering his people to be tempted unless his grace can make them gainers by it; Spurgeon diagnoses the soured heart as melancholy and choleric, its hard thoughts like stones in the kidneys, and marks at the twenty-fifth verse the turn from the glitter that had fascinated the man to the true gold that was his treasure.

Gill reports that the word for grieved means leavened, so that the man was in a ferment as a Latin playwright uses the phrase of one in anger, and that others render it inflamed; he takes the continual presence both of the man kept from departing finally and as a promise for hereafter, since the saints are always in union though not always in communion; offers three renderings of the guidance by counsel; and empties the heaven of the last verse of every other object of trust, the sun and moon and stars below and the angels and glorified saints above.

Clarke takes the confession of the twenty-second verse personally, that he felt as if he were a beast in stupidity for letting his mind be occupied with sensible things like the beasts that perish, applies the continual presence to his people as well as himself, and holds that the original of the twenty-fifth verse is more emphatic than the English, adding that no man can say it who has not taken God for his portion in reference to both worlds; Wesley keeps the grief to being deeply wounded with disquieting thoughts.

Ellicott gives the word for grieved literally, that the heart grew sour, corrects foolish to brutish in the following verse, and renders the second clause of the twenty-fifth that besides thee I have no delight on earth; Keil and Delitzsch keep to the sequence of the thought, which has passed from the standpoint of the end to the possession of God himself.

debates: What does the twenty-first verse say happened to the heart? Ellicott gives it literally, that it grew sour, and Spurgeon follows a reading to the same effect, working it into a diagnosis of black bile and hard thoughts like stones in the kidneys. Gill reports the same word as meaning leavened, so that the man was in a ferment as a Latin playwright uses the phrase of one in anger, and adds that others render it inflamed or made hot, not with the love of God but with wrath. Wesley and Clarke keep to the plain sense of a mind wounded by its own thoughts.
outliers: Henry finds an old riddle unriddled in the passage, meat coming out of the eater, since the temptation itself was turned to profit.
Spurgeon presses the medical figure of the twenty-first verse, making the man’s hard thoughts like so many stones in his kidneys.
Clarke sets a condition on the twenty-fifth verse, that no man can say it who has not taken God for his portion in reference to both worlds.
Gill notes that the question of the twenty-fifth verse may also be rendered as asking who is on my side in heaven.
themes: counsel, and the ways of taking it

26.pericope_label: My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever: it is good for me to draw near to God

schools.summary: Gill canvasses four occasions for the failing of flesh and heart and prefers the last, a body emaciated by sickness and a heart failing at the point of death, since the heart is said to be the first that lives and the last that dies; he defines the distance of the twenty-seventh verse as alienation from the life of God and from righteousness; and he hears in the last verse a recent experience rather than a maxim, dividing the good into the honourable, the pleasant and the profitable.

Clarke makes the failing the prospect of death, when natural courage fails and only supernatural support avails, renders the answering clause as the rock of my heart and takes the portion for an inheritance above rather than below; at the twenty-seventh verse he denies that perishing means annihilation, calling that as great a heresy, though scarcely so absurd, as holding that the pains of the lost are corrective, and arguing that if punishment is not eternal there is presumptive evidence that glory will not be either; at the last verse he sets those who draw near against those who are far off and reports a clause four versions add which no Hebrew copy acknowledges; Wesley notes that revolt to work wickedness is called going a whoring in Scripture.

Ellicott corrects the sense of the works of the last verse, which are not God’s doings but the works prescribed to the writer, the messages entrusted to him, here the conclusions he had reached and the truths revealed to him in contrast with the false opinions from which he had been freed; Keil and Delitzsch give the verse without comment, printing the text alone where the others expound.

debates: What does perishing mean at the twenty-seventh verse? Clarke raises the question himself and answers it against annihilation: the word is generally used of coming to nothing, and some apply it so to the finally impenitent, but he asks where that is found in Scripture and replies, in no part properly understood, since the wicked shall be in their own place though none of them shall be found in the new heavens and the new earth. He calls the opinion as great a heresy, though scarcely so absurd, as the belief that the pains of the lost are corrective, and adds that if punishment is not eternal there is presumptive evidence that glory will not be eternal either. Gill and Wesley keep to the description of the men rather than the duration of their end.
outliers: Clarke uses the last verses of the psalm to argue against the annihilation of the finally impenitent, and against the belief that the pains of the lost are corrective.
Ellicott takes the works of the last verse to be not God’s doings but the messages entrusted to the writer, the very conclusions this psalm has reached.
Gill supports his reading of the failing heart with the physicians, that the heart is the first thing that lives and the last that dies.
Clarke reports a closing clause about the gates of the daughter of Sion which four versions add and no Hebrew copy acknowledges, remarking that it makes a better finish.
themes: the first to live and the last to die
a rock for a failing heart
an ending no Hebrew copy has
